text:
Turnip.
DIFFICULTY
Easy
1/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Spring / Summer / Autumn

Turnips are faster-growing and less hardy than swedes. Pull them young for mild, juicy spring roots, sow as a catch crop after summer harvests, or store small autumn roots for winter stews. They usually have white flesh and leaves arising directly from the root, without a raised neck. Early types take 60–80 days, sometimes almost as fast as radishes. Autumn roots take longer; eat them before the hardest winter weather. Some varieties also give edible turnip tops.

Quick facts
Harvest

Mar – Jun; Sep – Nov

Germination

6–10 days

Sowing depth

About 1/2 in.

Row spacing

9-12 in. between rows.

Ready in

About 6–12 weeks from sowing; baby roots may be ready sooner

Sow

Mar–Apr for early roots. Aug for storage. Early Sep in mild areas gives smaller roots.

Yield (10 ft row)

early varieties: 7 lb; maincrop varieties: 12 lb

Plant spacing

Between plants: Baby 4 in.; early 6 in.; maincrop 9 in.; tops 4 in.

Recommended varieties
EARLY
Tokyo Cross

Quick white roots for tender, young harvests and short-season successions.

EARLY
Purple Top Milan

Traditional flat white roots with purple tops. Pick young for quick crops.

EARLY
Sweetbell F1

A modern white turnip for mild, tender young roots.

MAINCROP
Golden Ball

Yellow flesh with fuller flavour for cooking, alongside white summer turnips.

EARLY
Snowball

Quick-growing, round, white-fleshed turnip for harvesting young.

Key risks
Flea beetle

Late spring and early summer sowings can be badly peppered by flea beetle.

Checked growth / poor root quality

Turnips, swedes and radishes need steady, quick growth.

Cabbage root fly

Maggots tunnel the roots.

Woody roots

Heat, drought, overcrowding, starvation or leaving spring roots too long makes roots woody, fibrous or strong-tasting.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
96
ROOT CROPS

Pull baby roots young.

Thin crowded rows by harvesting the larger roots.

Avoid checks to growth.

Keep the crop moist, weed-free and growing quickly.

Soil & preparation
Use fertile, well-drained soil in cool weather. Heat/drought cause bolting and woody roots.
Firm, fine seedbed; add compost ahead. Drain wet ground.
Sowing & planting
Sow a fine drill
Thin for your crop
Sow 

Make shallow drills and sow thinly, cover lightly and keep moist. Sow short rows for baby roots and repeat in cool weather. Use cloches for early sowings and avoid hot, dry spells.

Looking after the crop
Thin while seedlings are small: baby roots need less room than storage roots. Pull larger baby roots first so smaller ones can grow on.
Weed carefully and water in dry weather. Poor drainage, hunger and crowding also check growth and reduce tenderness.
Fine mesh guards against flea beetle and root fly, especially in late spring/early summer. Net autumn plants against birds. Check caterpillars and damaged root cores; moisture and rapid growth help plants withstand damage.
Harvesting & storage
Pull spring roots young, at golf-ball size or smaller for baby turnips, before summer heat hardens them. Take larger roots first from crowded rows so smaller ones grow on.
Lift autumn roots before severe frost. Twist off leaves and store sound maincrop roots in dry sand in a cool shed; use turnips before hardier swedes.
For spring greens, cut tops in March or April at about 5 in. high. Leave strong plants to resprout for further cuts.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Flea beetle	Tiny holes in young leaves.	Mesh seedlings; water to keep growth steady.
Cabbage root fly	Maggots tunnel roots.	Cover after sowing; discard badly damaged roots.
Woody roots	Hard, fibrous or strong roots.	Keep growth steady; pull spring roots young.
Boron deficiency	Grey-brown or hollow cores.	Confirm with a soil test; seek organic advice, never overdose.
Birds and caterpillars	Leaves stripped or chewed.	Net securely; pick off eggs and caterpillars.
Soft rot	Wet, slimy crowns; foliage collapses.	Remove affected roots; store only sound, undamaged roots.
Black rot	Yellow leaves; black veins or root rings.	Remove diseased plants; rotate and improve drainage.
Turnip mosaic virus	Twisted, mottled young leaves.	Remove infected plants; encourage aphid predators.
Final tips

Dual-purpose varieties also provide young edible leaves.

A small August sowing makes a useful catch crop.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
